vignette: The narrative of her life splits at a precise moment: the evening three years ago. She walks home from a late class. A misplaced key, a wrong turn down a dimly lit alley, a man who steps from the shadows. The assault is sudden, absolute, and over too quickly. When he finally walks away, she stands on the cold pavement, breathless and shaking. Her mind pulls itself out of her body to keep her from drowning. She walks the remaining miles home in a fog. Every streetlight feels like an interrogation lamp. Every passing car feels like a threat. The months that follow unspool in slow motion. She stops walking alone after dusk. She begins sleeping with the bedroom door locked, then the handle barricaded with a heavy book. Her partner learns to speak in a lower register, to always announce himself before reaching for her. She loves him, fiercely, but her body keeps its own ledger. When he touches her shoulder, she feels the phantom weight of another’s grip. When the television plays a certain type of scene, her pulse spikes before her mind registers why. She starts keeping a meticulous schedule, filling every hour with structure, because unpredictability feels like an open door to the past. Teaching becomes her anchor. She works as a private tutor now, meeting with high school students in the bright, quiet corner of a neighborhood library. She prepares lesson plans with careful precision, arranging markers, color-coding equations, speaking clearly about quadratic functions and historical texts. In those hours, she is fully present. The students’ questions ground her. But the sanctuary is fragile. A dropped chair leg makes her shoulders jerk. A hand brushing her arm while reaching for a book sends a cold current through her ribs. She has learned to sit with her back against the wall, her bag placed neatly at her feet, her breathing regulated through counting. She tells herself she is safe. She repeats it until her body believes it. Her days are measured in routines and rehearsals. She wakes before the alarm, eyes already open, scanning the room for exits. The night lingers in her bones. She drinks her tea standing by the window, watching the street below until the world fills with familiar movement. Her relationship has deepened in quiet ways; her partner leaves notes, learns her rhythms, never pushes the boundaries she has set. Yet some evenings, when the house grows still, she sits on the edge of the bed and watches the shadow of the window frame stretch across the floor. She hums the same lullaby her mother taught her, a low vibration in her chest, wondering how to carry the weight of what happened without letting it dictate the shape of her days. Now, at thirty-five, she moves through her life with deliberate care. She corrects a student’s handwriting with gentle encouragement. She laughs at a colleague’s joke, the sound catching in her throat before settling. She notices the way the afternoon light falls across her desk, the smell of old paper, the steady rhythm of her own breath. The past does not leave, but it no longer occupies every room. She is here, in this chair, in this room, in this moment, learning how to stay.
